# Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty {.unnumbered}

Two applicants reach the final interview. One tells a vivid story about rescuing a failing project; the other has a quieter record of steady performance. The story makes the first applicant easier to imagine succeeding, yet the quieter record may offer the better guide to future work. The committee needs to predict performance while a memorable interview pulls its attention toward a different question: who feels convincing now?

We need shortcuts because time and information are limited. Some make good use of reliable patterns; others give weight to what is memorable, easy to process, or convenient to believe. The chapters in this part examine both possibilities. They begin with intuitive judgment, then show how comparison and presentation affect the answer, before introducing statistical tools that make an impression testable.

The task is to know what an intuitive answer rests on. A base rate may improve a forecast, a denominator may expose a misleading percentage, and a record of earlier predictions may reveal confidence that has outrun accuracy.

## Questions to carry forward

- Which observation is doing most of the work in my judgment?
- When would that observation be a reliable guide?
- What comparison or evidence could change my answer?

A well-calibrated probability still leaves a choice to make. Part III asks how we value its consequences, especially when risk, delay, and repeated behavior enter the picture.
